item.title: Xinhua Commentary: Chinese modernization forges new opportunities for Asia-Pacific community
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
BEIJING, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- As China hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this year, three words stand out in its agenda: openness, innovation and cooperation. They are also three important ways in which Chinese modernization is creating new opportunities for the Asia-Pacific. This is particularly relevant as the Asia-Pacific Media Forum 2026 brings together media representatives to discuss the region's development and future. While the discussion goes beyond the media community, it highlights a pressing question: how development opportunities can translate into broader prosperity across the region. Openness means more opportunities to connect with China's growth. The Chinese modernization is taking place in an economy deeply integrated with the Asia-Pacific. China accounts for more than a quarter of APEC's combined GDP, while its trade and investment ties with regional economies continue to strengthen. The scale of China-ASEAN economic ties offers a telling example. In 2025, trade between China and ASEAN reached 7.55 trillion yuan, or more than 1 trillion U.S. dollars, up 8 percent year-on-year. ASEAN remained China's largest trading partner. As Chinese consumers demand more diverse goods and services and Chinese industries continue to upgrade, this large and growing market creates space for businesses across the region. Openness therefore does more than keep trade flowing. It allows China's development to generate demand and opportunities beyond its borders. Innovation means more possibilities for new growth. Chinese modernization is also being driven by technological progress and the green and digital transformation of the economy. In 2025, China's expenditure on research and development reached 3.93 trillion yuan, or about 551 billion dollars, up 8.1 percent from the previous year and equivalent to 2.8 percent of GDP. For the Asia-Pacific, the significance of such innovation goes beyond the technologies themselves. A vast market and strong industrial capacity can help turn new technologies into products and applications on a large scale. As green and digital technologies become more widely applied, they can create new demand, new industries and new opportunities for businesses across the region. This is closely aligned with APEC's own innovation agenda, as APEC economies are discussing open innovation, cross-border knowledge flows and cooperation in areas including artificial intelligence, digital transformation and green development. Cooperation means turning opportunities into shared gains. No economy can address today's development challenges alone. For the Asia-Pacific, where economies differ widely in their levels of development, industrial structures and capabilities, cooperation can help turn differences into complementarity and make development more inclusive. Chinese modernization places strong emphasis on coordinated development and common prosperity. In practice, China's manufacturing capacity, technological advances and large market can complement the resources, industries and markets of other Asia-Pacific economies, creating more room for trade, investment and industrial cooperation. This is particularly important for the Asia-Pacific, where APEC's 21 economies differ widely in their levels of development and economic structures. The region's diversity need not be a divide. With cooperation, it can become a source of strength. As APEC economies look ahead, openness can widen access to markets, innovation can open up new sources of growth, and cooperation can turn differences into shared strengths. Together, they can help translate development opportunities into tangible benefits for people across the region. This is how Chinese modernization can make a meaningful contribution to the Asia-Pacific: by opening up more space for shared development and helping turn the vision of an Asia-Pacific community into reality. ■

item.title: Exhibition bridges gap between centuries-old Chinese encyclopedia, public
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
LANZHOU, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- An art gallery in Lanzhou, capital of northwest China's Gansu Province, has turned a colossal ancient encyclopedia into something anyone can enjoy. Instead of displaying dense classical Chinese that only scholars can master, it exhibits 122 images from this seldom-presented 18th-century compendium, such as a sketch of an ancient Indian unicorn, a star map nearly a millennium old, and the private scribbles of a stern, diligent emperor. These images form part of a years-long project to digitize a copy of the Siku Quanshu, which translates as the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, one of the most comprehensive collections of Chinese classical works in Chinese history. Compiled during the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911), the book runs to nearly 800 million characters across thousands of volumes, covering everything from Confucian philosophy to farming techniques. Seven copies were originally produced, but only three and a half survive today, preserved in Beijing, Taipei and Lanzhou, respectively. For decades, this massive treasured book was locked away. To better preserve its copy, Lanzhou built a dedicated library in an underground repository with constant temperature and humidity. In 2021, a project was launched to digitize it. By the end of May 2022, the scanning work of the text was finished, and the project moved into data processing. A team of young editors then spent more than two years checking the data page by page, and along the way, they discovered something unexpected: the playful side of the massive and complex text. "Most people think such a book would be too difficult to read," said Zhang Yang, deputy director of the digital publishing center at Duzhe Publishing & Media, the project's lead. "But as we went page by page, we found plenty of vivid images that could spark modern readers' curiosity." What started as a routine check soon turned into a curatorial mission. The team selected 122 of the most striking images and organized them into twelve sections, covering tea culture, astronomy, architecture, medicine, costume, and even weapon-making. The editors gave the sections funny titles such as "Ancient Gardening Know-How" and "Ancient Stargazing Guide," bridging the gap between centuries-old social life and the modern day. One section is called "World Mystery Box," featuring images from geographical works by Western missionaries during the Qing Dynasty. These images depict the Colosseum in Rome, the Colossus of Rhodes, and exotic and mythical creatures, such as lions and mermaids. "We had long heard of the Siku Quanshu by name, but this is our first time seeing it up close," said Liang Tao, a visitor from Xi'an. "It's both fun and awe-inspiring." That reaction echoes the goal of the exhibition. Song Xuejuan, who heads the digitization project, said the exhibition "transforms 'static preservation' into 'dynamic sharing', and turns an academic treasure into a public experience." For a long time, there was a disconnect between traditional culture and younger generations. In recent years, however, new technologies, fresh perspectives, and innovative storytelling have helped connect ancient heritage with contemporary trends. The Mogao Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site dating back to the 4th century, also in Gansu, are an example. In the 1980s, local researchers began exploring digital documentation. Today, they have completed high-precision digital capture of 323 caves. The images rendered on screen are now even clearer than what the naked eye can see on site, revealing details that once required climbing ladders to inspect. Another example is the immersive interactive digital exhibition of oracle bone inscriptions, held in Tianjin in April. Using artificial intelligence and mixed reality technologies, it allowed visitors to experience the ancient ritual of oracle bone divination. The Lanzhou gallery said it had previously received only a few hundred visitors per day on average. But since this new image exhibition launched, it has seen attendance surge to over 3,000 on peak days. Among the crowds were many children accompanied by parents. For Song's team, they were no longer editors merely checking for data errors, but rather communicators sharing the treasures with the public. "I used to think the Siku Quanshu was unreachable," said Song Jia'ni, a 34-year-old editor on the team. "But once you get into it, you will realize you don't have to begin with big history. One picture, or one detail, is enough to hook you." ■

item.title: Asia-Pacific SMEs seek new growth through AI, deeper connectivity
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
GUANGZHOU, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- On a production line at Seng Fong Holdings Berhad in Malaysia, a robotic arm grips a 35-kilogram block of rubber, with 3D cameras, laser scanners and AI algorithms serving as its "eyes" and "brain." The setup is designed to tackle a longstanding challenge in the traditionally labor-intensive rubber processing industry. Rubber blocks coming out of drying ovens vary in shape, making them difficult for conventional robotic systems to handle. Developed by an AI company in China's southern Guangdong Province, the solution has enabled the Malaysian rubber processor to automate more of the handling process, cutting labor costs by 20 to 30 percent while improving management efficiency, according to the company's chairman. The case points to a broader shift taking place across the Asia-Pacific. AI is creating new opportunities for SMEs to innovate, while deeper regional connectivity is helping them turn technological advances into new sources of growth. That trend was reflected at the 32nd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Small and Medium Enterprises Ministerial Meeting, held on Friday in Guangzhou, capital of Guangdong, as officials from APEC economies gathered to explore how technological innovation can empower SMEs and drive their further development. SMEs are a major pillar of the regional economy. As technological and industrial transformation accelerates and global supply chains undergo profound changes, AI and other emerging technologies are creating both new opportunities and new challenges for SMEs across the Asia-Pacific. AI-powered robotics are opening up new pathways for the digital transformation of SMEs, while open-source technologies are further lowering the barriers to technology access and application, enabling more businesses to participate in technological innovation, said Yang Qian, co-founder and chief operating officer of the Shenzhen-based embodied AI startup X Square Robot, at a parallel forum held alongside the ministerial meeting. "What once required six months, costly computing power and a professional team can now be done in three days with a workstation and an idea," she said. "This gives SMEs, for the first time, a more level playing field with industry giants in innovation." Yet SMEs across the region still face challenges, such as high digital transformation costs and talent shortages, highlighting the need for greater regional cooperation. Kwon Jong-hyun, vice chairman of the Beijing Chapter of the World-OKTA, cited embodied intelligence as an example, saying China's strengths lie in scale and speed, while those of the Republic of Korea lie in precision and reliability. Such cooperation, he said, is not simply about adding strengths together, but about multiplying their impact by combining complementary capabilities. China's experience in supporting SMEs' digital transformation offers one example. The latest move came on Friday, when the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released an action plan to support AI entrepreneurship among SMEs for 2026-2028. The plan aims to foster more than 10,000 technology-based and innovative SMEs, more than 2,000 "little giant" firms, as well as a number of gazelle companies and unicorns. Beyond domestic efforts, China is also seeking to extend AI cooperation through technology sharing and practical collaboration. It has announced that it will provide 5,000 opportunities for AI training and seminars for developing countries over the next five years. It is also advancing the establishment of AI application cooperation centers with ASEAN countries, with overseas branches in Laos, Malaysia and Vietnam already operational. These centers promote cross-border cooperation in large models, the data industry, and smart agriculture, bringing Chinese solutions together with local partners. China stands ready to work with all parties to help more SMEs thrive and grow, Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing said in a speech delivered at the opening ceremony of the meeting. The country is enhancing its policy support for SMEs and strengthening practical cooperation with APEC economies to jointly boost the high-quality development of SMEs, Zhang added. ■

item.title: Xinhua Communication Effectiveness Evaluation Index System releases report on APEC narratives
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
SHENZHEN, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Xinhua Communication Effectiveness Evaluation Index System on Saturday released Chinese and English versions of a report providing insights into APEC narratives at the Asia-Pacific Media Forum held in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. Titled Sharing Inspiring Asia-Pacific Stories, Contributing China's Constructive Solutions -- Insights into APEC Narratives Based on the Asia-Pacific Communication Index, the report was compiled based on multilingual data resources and intelligent research and analysis technologies of the Xinhua Communication Effectiveness Evaluation Index System. The report takes the period from 2023 to the first half of 2026 as the research cycle and selects over 200,000 pieces of information samples disseminated by more than 200 mainstream media outlets in the Asia-Pacific region. In the report, a quantitative assessment system based on four dimensions, namely communication heat, communication breadth, communication depth, and communication attitude, is established to assess the communication effect of the APEC concept across the region, identify narrative characteristics and communication patterns among Asia-Pacific media outlets, and objectively present public opinion trends and the evolution of Asia-Pacific cooperation under the new situation. The report notes that the communication model of APEC topics is undergoing profound changes, gradually shifting from the "annual meeting event-based communication" to "regular value-based discussion." The shift responds to the common aspirations of all economies to seek development, effectively consolidating long-term regional cooperation consensus and promoting widespread dissemination of the Asia-Pacific community vision. According to the report, openness, innovation and cooperation have emerged as the main themes of APEC communication. Among them, in-depth interpretations of "openness" account for the largest share; "innovation"-related topics lead in growth rate; and "cooperation" has the broadest reach and the strongest foundation of regional consensus. The three themes reinforce one another, continuously building consensus on regional development and creating a favorable international public opinion environment for building the Asia-Pacific community. Given the complex regional environment, the report stresses that deepening synergies and consolidating communication efforts of media outlets across the region are of great practical significance. China will continue to deepen dialogue and cooperation with Asia-Pacific economies, build bridges for mutual trust and communication, and work with Asia-Pacific media outlets to tell the Asia-Pacific stories of openness and inclusiveness, innovation-driven development, and win-win cooperation, contributing to the sustainable prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region. ■

item.title: Direct Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb flight opens new gateway to Central, Eastern Europe
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
* Air China now serves 27 European destinations with nearly 260 weekly flights between the two continents, with the Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route adding another thread to this growing network. * For Croatia, where tourism accounts for about one-fifth of GDP, the direct flight is a long-awaited gateway to the world's largest outbound tourism market. For Romania, it restores a connection that has been absent since 2003. And for Chinese travelers, it offers a new, hassle-free entry point to the wider Balkan region. by Xinhua writers Yao Yulin, Ma Zhen and Li Xuejun BUCHAREST/ZAGREB, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Air China launched its maiden Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb flight on Friday, restoring direct passenger links between China and Romania after more than two decades and inaugurating the first-ever scheduled passenger service between China and Croatia. Operating three times a week, the new route comes as Central and Eastern Europe -- known for its Adriatic coastline, medieval towns and rich cultural heritage -- is attracting growing interest from Chinese travelers. Travel has become more convenient than ever following China's unilateral visa-free policy for ordinary citizens of both Romania and Croatia. For Croatia, where tourism accounts for about one-fifth of GDP, the direct flight is a long-awaited gateway to the world's largest outbound tourism market. For Romania, it restores a connection that has been absent since 2003. And for Chinese travelers, it offers a new, hassle-free entry point to the wider Balkan region. VISA-FREE BENEFITS China and Romania once enjoyed direct air links, with Air China operating the route until 1994 and Romania's TAROM taking over until its suspension in 2003. For the next 23 years, travelers had to transit through third countries, turning a straightforward journey into a half-day ordeal. The new Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route has finally restored that missing link. The timing is no coincidence. In November 2024, China expanded its unilateral visa-free policy to include Romania and Croatia, along with seven other countries. Ordinary passport holders from both nations can now stay in China for up to 30 days without a visa for tourism, business, family visits or transit. The results have been striking. Around 35,000 Romanian citizens traveled to China in 2024, twice the figure recorded a year earlier. In the first seven months of 2025 alone, nearly 36,000 Romanians visited China, up 78 percent year-on-year, according to the National Association of Travel Agencies in Romania. Dan-Horia Maxim, Romania's ambassador to China, described the restored direct flights as "a major diplomatic and economic success aimed at bringing our communities closer together" in a press release. Chen Feng, China's ambassador to Romania, told Xinhua that the resumption of regular direct passenger flights has been a shared aspiration of the Chinese and Romanian peoples and reflects sustained joint efforts on both sides. "It is expected to help further strengthen bilateral economic and trade cooperation, deepen cultural and people-to-people exchanges, promote mutual understanding, and inject fresh momentum into the sustained and healthy development of China-Romania relations," Chen added. For Croatia, the numbers tell a story of promise still waiting to be fulfilled. In 2024, the country welcomed over 250,475 Chinese tourist arrivals, up more than 41 percent from the previous year. Yet that figure remains barely half of the pre-pandemic peak of some 490,000. Industry insiders view the new air link as a key step toward unlocking further growth. Qi Qianjin, China's ambassador to Croatia, called the route "the first direct flight in the history of the two countries and the latest achievement in deepening bilateral relations," adding that it would "significantly reduce travel time and costs, further unleash cooperation potential, and promote exchanges in trade, tourism, culture, sports and people-to-people ties." For China, the route fits into a broader pattern of deepening air connectivity with Central and Eastern Europe. Air China now serves 27 European destinations with nearly 260 weekly flights between the two continents, with the Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route adding another thread to this growing network. BALKAN HUB Kristjan Stanicic, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (CNTB), described the air link as "an important step forward" that "opens up additional opportunities for Croatian tourism to position itself more strongly on the large and promising Chinese market." He said Croatia is reaching out to Chinese visitors "through its exceptional diversity, but also through an authentic experience of our country, the local way of life, tradition and values." The CNTB, through its Shanghai office, plans to continue working with Chinese partners to "enable Chinese guests to get to know our homeland, its heritage and people in a quality and deeper way," Stanicic added. Dubrovnik, Split, Zadar and the capital Zagreb remain among the most popular Croatian destinations for Chinese tourists, but industry observers believe the new route could broaden that map. Leon Jiang, president of the Balkan Chinese Tourism Association and the Croatian Chinese Tourists Guide Association, said that direct access eliminates the inconvenience of transfers, making travel easier for both Chinese tourists heading to the Adriatic and Croatians interested in visiting China. Romania, too, stands to benefit significantly from the restored air link as the new route responds to long-standing calls from the tourism industry and provides infrastructure to meet growing two-way travel demand. In the first half of 2025 alone, Romania welcomed 21,682 Chinese tourists, the highest number of Asian visitors on record. With direct flights now in operation, the bottleneck that once held back the market's full potential is being removed. Romania has been actively positioning itself to capture a larger share of the Chinese outbound market. In May, Romania made its debut at ITB China in Shanghai, one of the most important B2B travel trade events dedicated to the Chinese market. The delegation promoted destinations including Bucharest, Transylvania and the monasteries of Bucovina. Earlier in October 2025, the China Tourism Fair was held at the Chinese Cultural Center in Bucharest, bringing together over 100 representatives from the tourism, culture and education sectors of both countries. Zagreb's strategic location also gives the route broader regional significance. Ljubo Jurcic, professor of economics and former Croatian minister of economy, pointed out that Chinese travelers arriving in Zagreb can easily continue to Italy and Austria, while the Adriatic coast is only a short journey away. Jurcic added that the route also signals Chinese interest in expanding cooperation with Croatia beyond tourism. "Croatian business people have long considered China an interesting market, because China is today the largest and most influential country in the world when it comes to business," he said. "Unfortunately, Croatian business people were not turned to China in time, but today that is changing." ■

item.title: Xi urges greater efforts to nurture capable young people for socialist cause
item.description:

BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Congratulating a popular national children's radio program on its 70th anniversary, Chinese President Xi Jinping urged professionals in children's culture to redouble efforts in nurturing a new generation of capable young people for the socialist cause. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the call in a congratulatory letter sent Friday to China Media Group's program named Xiaolaba, or Little Trumpet. He praised the program's 70-year commitment to "telling good stories to children," which have accompanied generations of young listeners as they grew up. Xi called on the program's team and professionals in children's culture to fulfill the mission of fostering virtue through education, keep pace with the times, tap deeply into the rich cultural resources, and devote themselves to creating more excellent and popular works that promote the true, the good and the beautiful among children. He urged greater efforts to nurture a new generation of capable young people with sound moral grounding, intellectual ability, physical vigor, aesthetic sensibility, and labor skills, who will be able to contribute to and carry forward the socialist cause. Launched on Sept. 4, 1956, Xiaolaba is the first radio program in the People's Republic of China dedicated to preschool children. It has since grown into a flagship program spanning radio, television, new media and in-school broadcasting. ■
